title: Does this look good enough to release?
author: vigridzki
selftext:
The game is built with a lot of help from Claude. I am a professional game programmer and work for an established company but for my personal project I wanted to see how far can I push AI workflows.

The game features:

Procedural prefab generation - phased out for voxel based models where available. Supports a generated and authored creation path.

Procedural track generation - builds and stitches together track fragments, and validates them for the ability to pass them, taking into account ship speed, maneuverability, jump range, and energy (“fuel”) drain along the length of the track, and takes into account collectibles that grant energy.

Difficulty ramp - the game has 5 “biomes”, 7 “zones” each, with increasing difficulty achieved by introducing hazards, obstacles and track mutators that make the track harder / unique.

Procedural music generation - it has a music director / composer that is fed with song structures, and it connects them together reacting to in-game events that contribute to “intensity” of the music. It supports different BPM and fancy time signatures. It harmonizes all the tracks (video lacks sound - even though it is „correct” I don’t like it yet).

Procedural instrument synthesis - all instruments work like a VST, support around 20 filters and processors, and 32 simultaneous voices.

Procedural SFX - baked on start.

Procedural engine sounds - simulated in real time.

It targets Steam Deck and Steam Machine with these performance goals (which it achieves):

\- Sub 2 seconds game load time to ready the start menu.  
\- Sub 150ms track generation on play.  
Instant replay of a failed track.  
\- 120FPS @ 4K resolution on Steam Machine with less than 1% frame hitches (upscaling from 86%)  
\- 90FPS @ 1280x800 resolution on Steam Deck with no frame hitches.

It started as a test if it could write a game like DOS game Skyroads (1993), with some mechanics from Race The Sun (2013) in 3 weeks. Then I showed it to a couple of people and they enjoyed playing it so it is stretching now into third month of development.

replies.author: CalSmally
replies.body:
Thats an overly harsh response. You're right that polish is important and takes a lot of time... But I've been working in the game industry for over 20 years making games the traditional way, and I've seen plenty of really well made games here in this thread and online that were developed with the help of AI in less than 3 months. Are they deep AAA titles with 50 hours of gameplay? No, but I don't think OP said that was their goal.

You can't really tell from watching a video whether or not the actual gameplay is fun or polished, or how satisfying the metagame feels, anyway. 

OP: I like the visuals, the simplified Tron style art and effects in the video. The pacing seems about right. One thing I would say from watching the video is the physics look a little floaty... Personally, I like racing games where the physics feel a little bit heavier.

Another thing to think about with racing games is adding some variety to the levels with gameplay beats. For example, have a section that's twisty followed by a section that's straight where you can go really fast. Or think about transitions through different environments, like an industrial section with lots of pipes and machinery, transitioning into a commercial section with neon signs.

replies.author: vigridzki
replies.body:
I really appreciate your comment and feedback. As for the floatiness - at some point I added verticality to the levels and the game became more fun (to me). What I think it’s lacking is more rewards for flight and shenanigans you could do with it. I think having more alternative vertical flight paths will address this somehow. I do agree at times the flight feels unjustified.

On your comment about timelines - I’ve been shocked how fast was I able to get the first prototype running (hours). I’ve been polishing the game ever since, experimenting without guilt, and throwing away things that didn’t work. It’s a completely different way of working.

As for level variety - I think I will leave handcrafted levels and the design control they  grant for another game. The levels I have get their variety from introducing different hazards and obstacles, and from totally different look across 5 different „biomes”. But changing them to feel more like a classic racing game is out of scope for this project, it’s flying forward, avoiding obstacles and taking sharp turns for this one, not for optimizing the laps.

Thank you so much for the rare, constructive feedback.

replies.author: CalSmally
replies.body:
>I’ve been polishing the game ever since, experimenting without guilt,

☝️ This is exactly what I love about AI use in game dev, too. 

In the olden times you'd make your best guess about what you thought should work and then implement it, and tweak it as much as you could before you ran out of money or time. Or you'd spend a bunch of time implementing some new feature and then get attached to it and keep trying to make it work even after it's clear it's not working.

Being able to try a bunch of different stuff out quickly, and experiment, and toss out and replace systems that don't work -- in the long run, that's what's going to make "AI games" good.

replies.author: vigridzki
replies.body:
I am enjoying the hell out of being a junior game designer that this tool has enabled me to be :). There is only so much people can do with their time, and AI is an awesome enabler.

Wishing you a great day!

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body:
I don't think it's possible to answer that on a simple shirt video.
The game looks good and fun, but you should probably distribute some demo to close people (or full game to very close people) and ask them the same question.

You said you showed to some people, but I understood that they play a single session or two. If they play several hours and tell you that they won't refund the game then go release

replies.author: Kepler___
replies.body: I actually think the art style looks a lot better than a lot of the games that get posted. It's very charming, and the colors are good. Your UI needs to go through a lot right now, I actually think UI is the most consistently lacking aspect of most current AI projects, it will benefit from any amount of hand crafting you can add, even if its a pencil sketch for Claude. The others are right about things like the clipping, but if your main question is about art and color, I think you're on the right track there. The pacing looks really fun too.

replies.author: vigridzki
replies.body: Thank you. I’m glad you like the art style. The UI will definitely get some love.

comments.author: Giangero1
comments.body:
The police spaceships should detect buildings and fly around or above them. Right now, they just clip through buildings and walls, which honestly makes the game look like you don't care about polishing it.

Also, maybe instead of spamming a bunch of "+10 Air Time" HUD popups, it could all stack into one UI element that updates the number as you gain more points. You could even make it change color as the number gets higher.

Hope this helps! If I watched the recording more closely, I could probably find a lot more stuff that needs polishing, but yeah, I should be getting paid for this at this point lmao. You're getting free feedback, so that's all you get for now xd

replies.author: vigridzki
replies.body:
Thank you, and very good advice about stacking numbers into a single popup per type.

The ships will also get some collision love.
